scope: Research/design only; France 1970–1990 left formations (PS, PCF, Communist Old Guard, PSU). No game implementation.
historical_method: Tags separate documented party positions or bilateral precedents from plausible governing extrapolation and game-balance proposals. The January 1970 start predates the PS's 1971 Epinay unification. France left NATO's integrated command in 1966 but remained in the Alliance; all choices retain French national command. Foreign offers are proposals requiring recipient-player consent; they never change a foreign government, impose sanctions, or create mutual-war behavior. Accepted compacts create symmetric, lasting spirits and end for both sides on voluntary withdrawal, war between signatories, sanctions between signatories, or loss of a signatory. A government change does not end an accepted compact; it invalidates only a pending proposal if its mandate no longer holds.

groups.historical_baseline: PS / left-socialist governments from 1971 onward; do not backdate Mitterrand's Epinay leadership to the January 1970 start.

strategic_fork.title: Independent deterrent or negotiated disarmament

choice_a.design: Retain a nationally controlled nuclear deterrent and professional high-readiness cadre, with parliamentary oversight and a costly French-only readiness and maintenance burden. Benefits: readiness, command continuity, aviation/missile integration training. Cost: sustained defence outlays and less room for conventional force expansion.

choice_b.design: Adopt the disarmament current debated inside the PS: freeze new strategic delivery systems, preserve territorial defence, and redirect trained personnel and engineering capacity toward conventional reserves and civilian aerospace. Benefits: reserve depth, civilian conversion, arms-control credibility. Cost: lower immediate specialist readiness and no strategic modernization bonuses.

evidence: PS defense convention debate in 1978 records motions to retain nuclear weapons and NATO membership alongside amendments to abandon Mirage IV, Albion and Pluton; this was an internal split, not a single settled PS platform.
Mitterrand's 1981 statement defended deterrence as national independence; it documents a later governing choice, not the 1970 party position.
strategic_fork.narrow_follow_through: If retained, a one-use bonus can target the exact eligible French fighter or missile-system research in the active tree; if disarmed, target one eligible airframe/civilian-electronics technology. Never award generic military research or complete a project.

country_offers.label: Aerospace workshare compact
country_offers.basis: Airbus GIE founded in December 1970 with French SNIAS and West German Deutsche Airbus each holding 50%; later cross-border workshare widened.
country_offers.offer: Shared aerospace production standards, supplier qualification and engineering training; bilateral spirits improve aircraft production efficiency and civilian engineering capacity.
country_offers.tradeoff: France accepts workshare and export coordination, sacrificing unilateral control of some production decisions.

country_offers.label: Helsinki-era industrial and scientific exchanges
country_offers.basis: The 1975 Franco-Soviet declaration expressly covered industrial, scientific, technical and environmental exchange under the Helsinki framework.
country_offers.offer: Reciprocal engineering placements and selected civilian industrial methods; gain industrial process training and one-use bonus to a named eligible industry technology.
country_offers.tradeoff: Trade information and limited production interoperability for stronger East-West access; no nuclear or command secrets.

country_offers.label: CNRS–Federal research programme
country_offers.basis: The 1966 France–Yugoslavia treaty created annual or biennial scientific and technical programmes linking research institutions.
country_offers.offer: Reciprocal research placements and industrial-science projects; gain civilian R&D capacity and a one-use bonus in one named engineering/electronics technology.
country_offers.tradeoff: Benefits are gradual and civilian-led, with no immediate arms output.

country_offers.label: Scientific cooperation mission
country_offers.basis: France recognized the PRC in 1964; a bilateral scientific and technical cooperation agreement followed in 1978.
country_offers.offer: Limited reciprocal civilian research and technical training; improve research access and diplomatic reach.
country_offers.tradeoff: A narrow, slow programme with no assumed military alignment or shared doctrine.

groups.historical_baseline: PCF's Common Programme co-signatory role and 1970s debates; distinguish the PCF from the separate counterfactual Old Guard current.

strategic_fork.title: Regional citizen reserves or party-directed arms command

choice_a.design: Translate the 1972 Common Programme's six-month service, regionally organized trained reserves, and democratic rights for soldiers/cadres into a territorial-reserve institution. Benefits: lower personnel burden, reserve manpower and civil-defense capacity. Cost: weaker rapid expeditionary reach and more training coordination.

choice_b.design: Concentrate procurement planning and senior appointments in a centralized public arms authority, prioritizing production continuity and artillery/infantry readiness. Benefits: faster allocation, reliable planned output and staff coordination. Cost: less local discretion, more bureaucratic bottlenecks and weaker conversion flexibility.

evidence: The 1972 Common Programme is a proposal, not an enacted French reform; it specifies six-month service, trained regional reserves, democratic status for soldiers and cadre rights/reconversion.
The PCF's 1976 Congress abandoned the dictatorship-of-the-proletariat formula and affirmed a French democratic road, so post-1976 PCF governance should not be collapsed into Soviet orthodoxy.
strategic_fork.narrow_follow_through: Reserve route: one-use bonus to a specific eligible support-weapons/engineer technology. Central route: one-use bonus to a specific eligible artillery technology. No broad military-category bonus.

country_offers.label: Industrial and technical exchange
country_offers.basis: France and USSR maintained state-level scientific, technical, economic and cultural cooperation through the 1970s; the 1975 declaration names these sectors.
country_offers.offer: Reciprocal civilian industrial training and selected production methods; gain planned-industry throughput and one eligible industry research use.
country_offers.tradeoff: Greater dependence on negotiated East-West supply channels; no transfer of strategic weapons technology.

country_offers.label: Industrial standards and maintenance exchange
country_offers.basis: France and GDR signed an economic, industrial and technical cooperation agreement in Paris in 1973.
country_offers.offer: Reciprocal maintenance training, machine-tool practice and civilian electronics placements; improve maintenance resilience and one narrow industrial/electronics technology.
country_offers.tradeoff: Lower immediate expansion than a dedicated arms order; benefits center on repairability and process discipline.

country_offers.label: Civil engineering and mapping cooperation
country_offers.basis: A bilateral cartographic cooperation convention was signed in 1968; earlier agricultural education cooperation used French experts, training and equipment.
country_offers.offer: Reciprocal survey, engineering and technical-school placements; strengthen logistics mapping and engineer training.
country_offers.tradeoff: Civilian infrastructure and training consume capacity that could fund direct arms production.

country_offers.label: Mediterranean public-industry liaison
country_offers.basis: Proposed as a plausible Eurocommunist-era industrial dialogue; do not state that a state military treaty or shared PCF–Italian Communist Party policy existed.
country_offers.offer: Voluntary public-enterprise technical placements and repair-standard exchange; improve maintenance and industrial engineering.
country_offers.tradeoff: No guaranteed arms order or doctrinal alignment; gains are modest and conditional on acceptance.

groups.historical_baseline: Counterfactual playable Thorezian/Vermeersch-aligned Old Guard; it was not a separate governing party in 1970. Do not present its branch as actual PCF policy after 1976.

strategic_fork.title: Soviet-standardized mass army or autonomous French reserve

choice_a.design: Seek Soviet-standardized doctrine, staff education and equipment interoperability while retaining French political command. Benefits: specialist readiness and access to maintenance/training; cost: recurring dependence on foreign standards and reduced French procurement flexibility.

choice_b.design: Prioritize a mass conscript reserve, French-controlled depots and domestic artillery/vehicle maintenance. Benefits: manpower depth and sovereign repair capacity; cost: slower mobilization-to-readiness and higher domestic replacement burden.

evidence: A distinct Old Guard electoral government is alternate history. The real PCF remained internally tied to Soviet traditions but changed its public doctrine in 1976; the proposed branch deliberately explores the counterfactual of a hard-line current governing independently.
France's continuing national command after leaving NATO's integrated command in 1966 is a real invariant; do not turn Soviet cooperation into foreign command of French units.
strategic_fork.narrow_follow_through: Foreign-standard route may target one exact eligible electronics or artillery technology; domestic-reserve route one exact eligible artillery or armor-maintenance technology. Avoid bonuses to strategic nuclear weapons or generic combat stats.

country_offers.label: Staff college and maintenance mission
country_offers.basis: State scientific, technical and industrial cooperation is documented in the 1975 declaration; the specifically military mission is an alternate-history extrapolation.
country_offers.offer: Reciprocal staff observation and non-sensitive maintenance training; improve doctrine training and one narrow equipment technology.
country_offers.tradeoff: Interoperability with Soviet standards raises dependence and reduces French supplier freedom; French national command stays intact.

country_offers.label: Repair and machine-tool mission
country_offers.basis: 1973 France–GDR agreement covered economic, industrial and technical cooperation; military transfer is not established by that source.
country_offers.offer: Reciprocal industrial maintenance and machine-tool placements, not weapons transfer; improve depot repair and state-industry throughput.
country_offers.tradeoff: Lower procurement flexibility and no direct force-readiness grant.

country_offers.label: Non-aligned technical mission
country_offers.basis: French recognition in 1964 and the 1978 scientific/technical agreement provide a real diplomatic and science precedent; the proposed military channel is not documented.
country_offers.offer: Reciprocal civilian electronics and engineering placements; broaden technical access without assuming Beijing accepts Soviet orthodoxy.
country_offers.tradeoff: No doctrine match or arms supply assumed; modest research gain only.

country_offers.label: Industrial safety and aerospace standards
country_offers.basis: Franco-West German co-production through Airbus began in 1970; a 1980 presidential statement also announced joint tank and satellite projects.
country_offers.offer: Reciprocal aerospace and industrial-engineering placements; strengthen domestic production quality and one eligible aeronautics technology.
country_offers.tradeoff: Workshare and export coordination constrain unilateral choice; politically cross-bloc cooperation is an intentional Old Guard counterfactual.

groups.historical_baseline: PSU's distinctive self-management identity consolidates in 1972; its 1978 appeal later explicitly advocates demilitarized popular defence and rejection of civil and military nuclear power. Present the latter as a later platform development, not a January 1970 consensus.

strategic_fork.title: Professionally controlled defence or non-nuclear popular defence

choice_a.design: Keep a limited professional force under civilian/parliamentary control while protecting independent national command. Benefits: faster response and specialist technical skill. Cost: high personnel upkeep and tension with self-management constituencies.

choice_b.design: Build a territorially organized popular reserve, civil-protection engineering and industrial conversion; freeze nuclear expansion as the later PSU demilitarization current proposed. Benefits: local resilience, engineer training and civilian conversion. Cost: reduced expeditionary reach and slower specialist mobilization.

evidence: PSU self-management is documented as a defining programme adopted in 1972; worker control was distinguished from top-down state nationalization.

The 1978 Front Autogestionnaire appeal explicitly links self-management with demilitarized popular defence and rejection of civil/military nuclear power; applying it as a government programme is extrapolation.
strategic_fork.narrow_follow_through: Popular-defence route should reward one eligible engineer/support technology plus civil-protection or construction capacity; professional route should reward one eligible infantry-support or electronics technology.

country_offers.label: Workers' self-management and research exchange
country_offers.basis: Yugoslav 1974 constitutional institutions formalized worker self-management; France–Yugoslavia's 1966 science treaty linked research institutions through periodic programmes.
country_offers.offer: Reciprocal cooperative-enterprise exchanges, technical training and applied research; increase workforce skill and local production adaptability.
country_offers.tradeoff: Slower negotiated output and weaker central procurement coordination.

country_offers.label: Engineering schools and civil mapping
country_offers.basis: Documented cartographic cooperation and French-supported Algerian agricultural education/training provide precedents for technical capacity-building.
country_offers.offer: Reciprocal civil-engineering, survey and vocational training; improve engineer availability and logistics knowledge.
country_offers.tradeoff: Civilian placements tie up scarce specialists; no assumed military alignment.

country_offers.label: Non-aligned civilian science network
country_offers.basis: France recognized the PRC in 1964 and concluded a scientific and technical cooperation agreement in 1978.
country_offers.offer: Reciprocal public research and engineering placements; broaden civilian technical access.
country_offers.tradeoff: Long-horizon, non-military gains; no assumed common political programme.

country_offers.label: Aerospace and dual-use civil engineering
country_offers.basis: The 1970 Airbus GIE was created with equal French and West German stakes; joint output depended on negotiated workshare.
country_offers.offer: Reciprocal civil aerospace and industrial-engineering placements; raise technical capacity and civilian conversion potential.
country_offers.tradeoff: Shared standards and workshare limit unilateral industrial control, a direct tension with local autonomy.

Epinay reorganization in June 1971 and Common Programme signature with PCF in June 1972; guards against backdating unified PS to Jan 1970.
Internal split: deterrent retention/NATO alongside amendments to abandon Mirage IV, Albion and Pluton.
Mitterrand's 1981 justification for independent nuclear deterrence and national independence; later governing decision, not 1970 platform.

sources.type: PCF institutional retrospective by former senior party officials
sources.supports: Recounts the 1975 liberty charter, Marchais announcing abandonment of the dictatorship-of-the-proletariat notion in 1976, the democratic/French road, and continuing ties to Soviet models among some members. Partisan retrospective; distinguishes PCF from the proposed Old Guard.
PSU founding, post-1968 self-management identity, formal party commitment in 1972 and later political trajectory.
Self-management as PSU identity; distinguishes worker control from state nationalization and warns of technocratic/bureaucratic capture.

sources.type: primary party appeal archived by PSU institute
sources.supports: 1978 appeal for self-management, demilitarized popular defence and rejection of civil and military nuclear power; later development, not 1970 baseline.
France left integrated command in 1966 while remaining in Alliance; 1967 Ailleret–Lemnitzer and 1974 Valentin–Ferber arrangements maintained cooperation under French national command.
France–Yugoslavia scientific and technical cooperation treaty; CNRS/Federal Council institutional exchanges and annual or biennial work programmes; effective 1966.
Airbus GIE established 18 Dec 1970; French SNIAS and West German Deutsche Airbus initially held 50% each.
Franco-Soviet cooperation in industrial, scientific, technical, environmental, cultural and educational exchange under European security détente.
France–GDR economic, industrial and technical cooperation agreement signed in Paris, 19 July 1973; source does not establish military transfers.

Franco-Algerian cartographic cooperation convention signed 2 Aug 1968 and published in 1970.
French expert, training and equipment support for Algerian agricultural education; supports civilian capacity-building precedent.
Worker self-management, councils/delegates and associated institutional structures in the 1974 Yugoslav constitution; use as institutional precedent, not proof of easy export.
1980 announcement of France–FRG joint tank and satellite projects; only for Old Guard's deliberately counterfactual cross-bloc industrial contact.

design_rules: Keep each partner's spirits symmetric and lasting while the agreement remains valid; never set foreign party/government variables or force acceptance.
Named-country offers are fixed bilateral proposals, with the receiver's explicit accept/refuse choice. No mutual-war pact, sanction action, or foreign regime change.
Terminate both sides together on signatory war, sanctions between signatories, either-side withdrawal, or either government's change; do not grant war support or political alignment as a side effect.

Offer effects should match the evidenced domain; label military cooperation beyond civil/industrial treaty scope as counterfactual. Do not share nuclear weapon design, secret command, or unverified arms transfers.
Give mutually exclusive national routes different institutional consequences and real opportunity costs. Avoid repeated flat stability, political-power, research-speed or generic military-stat buffs.
Use existing exact eligible technologies only after checking local definitions; a focus should never complete a special project or award a generic category bonus.
